tldr: A low factual prediction error on past data doesn't help planning if the model cannot distinguish between outcomes of different actions. Addressing this issue, AD-WM introduces residual latent dynamics and predictor-level action-recovery regularization to make action-dependent differences stand out in latent space. It dramatically improves success from 3.7% to 52.0% on a challenging simulation benchmark, and boosts zero-shot real-world transfer success from 42.2% to 71.1% without any lab-specific fine-tuning.
hero_caption: Comparison between conventional JEPA-based world models and the proposed AD-WM. Traditional models get dominated by static features like the background; even with low prediction error, subtle differences among candidate actions vanish. AD-WM strongly preserves action-dependent latent changes, enabling the planner to pick the right action to reach the goal.
overview:
In visual Model Predictive Control (MPC), an agent uses a world model to predict "what happens if I take this action" in a latent space and selects the sequence of actions that gets closest to a goal image. Recently, world models based on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) have gained massive attention because they predict future representations directly in feature space rather than reconstructing pixel-level images.

However, there is a major catch. World models are typically trained to accurately predict factual transitions recorded in training data. But what MPC actually needs is counterfactual comparison: comparing what would happen if different alternative actions were taken from the exact same state. When static background features dominate the latent space, predicting "do nothing" (no state change) yields an apparently tiny mean squared error. As a result, the model boasts high factual accuracy while remaining blind to the difference between moving an arm toward an object versus moving it away, leading planning to fail.

To solve this, the authors propose AD-WM, an action-discriminative joint-embedding world model combining residual latent dynamics with an action-recovery objective. By training the model to recover the taken action from its own predicted transitions, the latent changes evaluated during planning are forced to retain distinctive action information. Furthermore, because these auxiliary recovery heads are discarded at test time, standard MPC planners can be used without any modification.

In experiments on OGBench-Cube under a challenging non-contact hard-start protocol, a matched LeWM baseline managed only a 3.7% success rate, while AD-WM reached 52.0%. Furthermore, when paired with a frozen pretrained visual encoder (V-JEPA 2) and evaluated zero-shot on a real Franka arm without any lab-specific adaptation, AD-WM boosted basic pick-and-place success from 42.2% to 71.1%.
contributions: Revealed a fundamental mismatch in JEPA-based MPC between achieving low factual prediction error and maintaining the quality of counterfactual action comparisons.

Proposed AD-WM, combining residual latent dynamics and action-recovery regularization (inverse dynamics and normalized recovery) to retain action information within predicted transitions without changing the MPC planner or inference pipeline.
Demonstrated that CEM-aligned elite regret strongly correlates with closed-loop control success, whereas whole-bank action ranking (CAD) and factual prediction error do not follow success ordering.
Outperformed the baseline in four out of five simulation environments and significantly improved zero-shot transfer success on a real Franka manipulator from 42.2% to 71.1%.

sections.heading: Why accurate predictions can fail at control: The trap of counterfactual comparison
sections.summary: JEPA-based world models are powerful tools for planning without pixel reconstruction, but high factual prediction accuracy does not guarantee good counterfactual differentiation between candidate actions. This paper introduces AD-WM to retain action details in predicted latent transitions, evaluated through diagnostic metrics aligned with CEM planning.
sections.details:
In visual robot control, world models that imagine future outcomes before acting are essential. Recently, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models (such as LeWM and V-JEPA 2-AC) have been widely adopted because they predict future representations directly in feature space instead of reconstructing images. During planning, they roll out latent trajectories and select the action sequence whose final state is closest to the goal image features.

However, a critical challenge arises. During training, the model only sees the factual transitions that actually occurred, and it is trained to minimize prediction error on those factual pairs. Because visual features are largely dominated by static backgrounds and unchanging environmental details, predicting almost no state change still yields a very low mathematical prediction error. Consequently, the subtle latent difference between an action moving toward a block and one moving away gets washed out, leaving the planner incapable of picking the right candidate (Figure F1).

Planning does not just require accurate factual tracing; it demands action-discriminative latent dynamics that preserve the differences between alternative choices. To achieve this, this work introduces AD-WM, combining a residual latent dynamics structure with action-recovery regularization on predicted transitions. Furthermore, to evaluate search behavior in optimizers like the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM), the authors introduce an "elite regret" diagnostic metric, shedding light on the true relationship between model metrics and closed-loop control success.

captions.F1: The importance of action discriminability when comparing candidate actions. In conventional models (top), low prediction error still results in collapsed action differences in latent space. In contrast, AD-WM (bottom) preserves action-dependent changes, enabling proper candidate selection.

sections.heading: Lineage of world models and action-aware representation learning
sections.summary: This section reviews latent world models, JEPA-based feature-predictive planning, and action-conditioned representation learning via inverse dynamics. AD-WM is unique because it injects counterfactual action discriminability directly at the predictor level without altering the inference-time planner.
sections.details:
This work builds upon three main research foundations:

### Latent World Models for Control
Prior approaches like PlaNet, Dreamer, and TD-MPC learn latent dynamics from images to perform planning or policy optimization. Recently, Transformer-based and diffusion-based world models have also emerged. This paper focuses on the setting of learning from offline datasets using only image goals without reward functions. In this context, the quality of predicted latent transitions directly governs the comparison accuracy of the planner.

### Feature-Predictive World Models (JEPA)
Models such as DINO-WM, LeWM, and V-JEPA 2 avoid the overhead of pixel-level reconstruction by predicting futures in feature space. However, JEPA representations inherently bias toward temporally slow-moving features, often overlooking subtle, action-dependent changes. While methods like Fast-LeWM (accelerating rollouts), Sub-JEPA (preventing representation collapse), and INTACT (using alternative optimizers) have been proposed, this work takes a direct approach: injecting action discriminability directly into the transitions generated by the predictor.

### Action-Aware Representation Learning
Inverse dynamics, which predicts the executed action from consecutive states, is a classic technique for extracting action-relevant features. However, existing methods mostly apply inverse dynamics to observed encoder representations. The key innovation in AD-WM is applying it to transitions generated by the predictor (the current latent state and the model's predicted next latent state). This directly backpropagates gradients that preserve action information into the very dynamics that MPC evaluates during rollouts.

sections.heading: How AD-WM works: Residual prediction and dual action-recovery losses
sections.summary: Residual latent dynamics help capture small state shifts, while inverse dynamics and conditional mutual information-inspired normalized recovery losses bind action details into predicted transitions. Auxiliary heads are discarded at test time, keeping standard MPC fully intact.
sections.details:
The overall architecture and inference flow of AD-WM are illustrated in Figure F2. The individual components operate as follows:

### III-A Problem Formulation
Given an offline dataset $\mathcal{D}=\{(o_t, a_t, o_{t+1})\}$, the goal is to learn an image encoder $z_t = e_\phi(o_t)$ and latent dynamics $\hat{z}_{t+1} = F_\theta(z_t, a_t)$. At test time, given a goal image $g$ with feature $z_g$, MPC minimizes the terminal cost $\hat{c}(a) = \|\hat{z}_{t+H} - z_g\|_2^2$ over candidate action sequences $a = a_{t:t+H-1}$. When state changes are small, an uninformative model predicting zero change still achieves low mean squared error, making action-discriminative dynamics vital.

### III-B Residual Latent Dynamics
Consecutive visual frames share substantial information. AD-WM preserves the current representation $z_t$ and uses action embedding $e_t = \psi_\rho(a_t)$ to predict only the latent displacement $\Delta \hat{z}_t = f_\Delta(z_t, e_t)$, setting $\hat{z}_{t+1} = z_t + \Delta \hat{z}_t$. This residual formulation introduces an inductive bias toward capturing localized, subtle changes.

### III-C Predictor-Level Action-Recovery Regularization
A residual structure alone does not guarantee distinct outcomes for distinct actions. To ensure this, two auxiliary objectives recover the action from generated transitions $[z_t, \hat{z}_{t+1}]$:
- **Inverse Dynamics (Inv)**: Recovers the original action embedding $e_t$ from the predicted next state $\hat{z}_{t+1}$ and current state $z_t$, optimized via $L_{\mathrm{inv}} = \|\hat{e}_t - \operatorname{sg}(e_t)\|_2^2$ (where $\operatorname{sg}$ denotes stop-gradient). Crucially, gradients flow back into the predictor parameters.
- **Normalized Action Recovery (MI)**: Action embeddings are normalized (zero mean, unit variance) across batch statistics. Motivated by a variational lower bound on conditional mutual information $I(\bar{e}_t; \hat{z}_{t+1} \mid z_t)$, this objective maximizes log-likelihood with a KL penalty toward a standard Gaussian. This locks action information into latent transitions robustly against scale variations.

### III-D Training and Planning
In simulation, the total training loss is the sum of factual prediction loss $L_{\mathrm{pred}}$, non-collapse regularization $L_{\mathrm{SIGReg}}$, and the two auxiliary losses $L_{\mathrm{inv}}$ and $L_{\mathrm{MI}}$. During inference (MPC), all auxiliary heads are discarded, and CEM conducts standard rollout evaluations. The planner itself remains completely unchanged.

### III-E Planning Diagnostic Metrics
To evaluate candidate comparison beyond simple prediction error, the authors define new metrics. In addition to CAD (Spearman rank correlation over the entire action bank), they introduce Best Elite Regret $R_k$ and Mean Elite Regret $\bar{R}_k$. These measure the normalized difference against ground-truth costs rolled out in the real environment for the top-$k$ elite action sequences selected by CEM.

captions.F2: The AD-WM training and planning pipeline. Left: During training, predicted transitions from residual dynamics are regularized by Inverse Dynamics (Inv) and Normalized Recovery (MI) auxiliary heads to preserve action information. Right: At test time, auxiliary heads are discarded, and standard CEM-MPC searches for action sequences that reach the goal.

sections.heading: Simulation and real-robot evaluations: Don't be fooled by low prediction error
sections.summary: Tested across five simulation environments and a real Franka arm, AD-WM boosts success from 3.7% to 52.0% on a challenging Cube task with no initial contact, and reaches 71.1% on real-world zero-shot transfer. Crucially, elite regret—not factual MSE—correlates with control success.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted across five simulation environments (Cube, Reacher, TwoRoom, PushT, Scene) and a physical Franka manipulator (Figure F3, Figure F5).

### IV-A & IV-B Simulation Results
On OGBench-Cube under the challenging non-contact hard-start protocol (P00 to P04) where the gripper does not touch the cube initially, the matched LeWM reproduction achieved only a 3.7% average success rate, whereas AD-WM achieved 52.0%. Even on P04 with the largest perturbations, AD-WM maintained 25.3%, significantly beating external baselines like INTACT (Direct: 10.0%, Actor-CEM: 10.7%). Across all five environments, AD-WM outperformed baselines in four: Cube (73.3% to 90.7%), Reacher (76.7% to 83.3%), TwoRoom (90% to 98%), and Scene (35.5% to 39.5%), with a minor dip in PushT (94% to 92%).

### IV-C Ablations
Dissecting components on Cube showed that from a 3.7% baseline, residual prediction alone improved success to 34.7%, and combining residual prediction with normalized recovery (Res+MI) jumped to 54.7%. While inverse dynamics (Inv) alone had a smaller, weight-sensitive contribution, residual prediction and information-theoretic regularization (MI) proved to be the two main drivers of success.

### IV-D Why Did It Work? Planning Diagnostics
Strikingly, factual prediction error (MSE) on the test set showed an inverted trend: LeWM (the lowest success rate) had the lowest MSE, while AD-WM (the highest success rate) had the highest MSE. Furthermore, whole-bank rank correlation (CAD) correlated negatively with closed-loop success ($\rho = -0.399$). In sharp contrast, elite regret over the top-30 CEM candidates ($-R_{30}$ and $-\bar{R}_{30}$) correlated strongly with closed-loop success ($\rho = 0.863$ and $0.810$). This proves that distinguishing the top elite candidates during search matters far more than overall prediction accuracy.

### IV-E Zero-Shot Transfer to Real Franka
Using a model post-trained on the DROID dataset without any environment-specific data, the authors evaluated zero-shot control on a Franka arm (Figure F5). For pick-and-place guided by a single camera and goal images, AD-WM achieved a 71.1% success rate compared to 42.2% for V-JEPA 2-AC. Per-object success improved across all objects (33.3% to 60.0%, 46.7% to 73.3%, and 46.7% to 80.0%), while erratic failures dropped dramatically.

sections.heading: Conclusion and open questions
sections.summary: AD-WM equips MPC world models with counterfactual action discriminability through residual dynamics and action-recovery regularization, showing significant gains in simulation and real-world transfer. Limitations include the scope of diagnostics and reliance on subgoals on the physical robot.
sections.details:
This paper presented AD-WM, an action-discriminative joint-embedding world model for counterfactual MPC. Moving away from purely minimizing factual prediction error, AD-WM pairs residual latent prediction with predictor-level action recovery, significantly enhancing candidate differentiation without requiring changes to the test-time planner.

Nevertheless, the authors acknowledge several limitations:
- Detailed diagnostic analysis (such as elite regret) was primarily conducted on Cube; on the Scene benchmark, gains were not statistically verified across 3 seeds ($p=0.13$).
- Auxiliary loss weights differed between simulation and real-world post-training, leaving automatic hyperparameter tuning as an open question.
- Physical robot experiments relied on hand-specified visual subgoals (grasp, lift, place), rather than performing fully autonomous, end-to-end long-horizon planning. Future work aims to reduce subgoal dependence and scale to broader tasks.

takeaways: A low factual prediction error (MSE) does not guarantee successful MPC control; background dominance can easily suppress subtle action differences.
Regularizing predicted latent transitions $[z_t, \hat{z}_{t+1}]$ to recover actions injects counterfactual discriminability without modifying the planner.
For sampling-based planners like CEM, elite regret on top candidates is a far more reliable indicator of closed-loop success than whole-bank ranking correlation (CAD).
Combining residual latent dynamics with mutual information-based regularization (MI) substantially boosts zero-shot transfer to real robots without domain adaptation.
limitations: Physical robot evaluations rely on manually provided visual subgoals (grasp, move, place), meaning fully autonomous long-horizon planning is not yet achieved.
In-depth diagnostic metrics were primarily validated on the Cube task, leaving room for further statistical verification on complex environments like Scene.
Auxiliary loss weights (such as $\lambda_{\mathrm{MI}}$) were tuned differently between simulation and real post-training, lacking a universal automated tuning rule.
